entities.name: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County (NHM), established in 1913 as the Museum of History, Science, and Art, is the largest natural history museum in the western United States — holding 35 million specimens including the world's largest collection of Ice Age megafauna from the La Brea Tar Pits, one of North America's most important dinosaur collections, and comprehensive Native California ethnographic collections. The museum's Urban Nature project transformed the surrounding campus into a biodiversity research site, discovering 30 new species within Los Angeles city limits.

The La Brea Tar Pits, in the heart of Los Angeles' Hancock Park district adjacent to the museum, are the world's richest Ice Age fossil site — with 3.5 million bones from over 600 species preserved in natural asphalt seeps over 50,000 years. The collections include complete skeletons of saber-toothed cats (Smilodon), dire wolves, Colombian mammoths, and ground sloths from the Pleistocene era. The tar pits were being actively excavated as recently as 2023 in conjunction with the Los Angeles Metro Purple Line extension.

The museum's Urban Nature project (2013-) documented 30 new species within Los Angeles city limits — including four new bee species, six new millipedes, and the urban coyote population — demonstrating that megacities contain undiscovered biodiversity. The project's data showed Los Angeles's urban canyon system (irrigated lawns, drainage channels, street trees) creates habitat for over 2,000 species, challenging assumptions about urban ecological sterility.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The NHM's La Brea Tar Pit collection — 3.5 million Ice Age specimens from the world's richest asphalt fossil site — provides the most complete record of North American Pleistocene ecology and the extinction event that ended the age of mammoths and saber-toothed cats.
